system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2163-11-25 21:51:00 to 2163-11-30 15:26:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

scan.  She would not attempt PO contrast due to fear of becoming 
more nauseous and vomiting.  Her left lower quadrant pain 
resolved over several days.  This may have been related to her 
fibromyalgia or musculoskeletal pain.
.
3. FIBROMYALGIA
The patient was initially put on IV pain medications due to her 
nausea and vomiting.  She was tried on IV Dilaudid which made 
her nausea worse so she was put on IV Morphine.  She was 
transitioned to PO Oxycodone and Morphine on the day after 
admission and fibromyalgia pain was controlled.  Narcotic pain 
medications were confirmed with her PCP who suggested that no 
changes be made to her pain regimen.  She was on Oxycodone 45mg 
PO q6hours and Morphine ___ 45mg PO q6hours PRN.  She was 
discharged with this regimen and no changes or escalation of 
pain medications were made.
.
HYPERTENSION
The patient was continued on her Nifedipine XL 60mg PO qday for 
her hypertension and blood pressure was controlled during this 
admission.
.
SEIZURE DISORDER
The patient was initially subtherapeutic on her phenytoin, 
___ from vomiting prior to admission.  She was initially put 
on IV Phenytoin 200mg, 200mg, 300mg q8 hours for total daily 
dose of 1000mg.  She was rechecked and levels were low so she 
was bolused 1000mg IV phenytoin.  Levels the following morning 
were therapeutic.  She was changed to her home dose of Phenytoin 
and will have her Phenytoin levels checked in 1 week.  She had 
no seizures while hospitalized.
.
HX OF DVT/PE
Ms. ___ was sub-therapeutic on her Coumadin on admission 
with an INR of 1.2.  She was restarted on her home dose of 
Coumadin 7.5mg and was discharged on this dose with instructions 
to have her labs rechecked in 1 week.  
.  
HYPOTHYROIDISM 
Patient was put initially on IV Levothyroxine 25mcg qday and 
then was transitioned to PO Levothyroxine 25mcg PO daily.  This 
was continued on discharge.
.  
TOBACCO ABUSE
The patient was put on a Nicotine patch for smoking cessation.  
At times she requested to leave the floor to smoke but was able 
to tolerate cravings with gum and did not leave the floor.
.
PROPHYLAXIS
She was given SC Heparin for DVT prophylaxis while 
sub-therapeutic on Coumadin.  She was put on her home dose of 
Omeprazole and a bowel regimen.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ female with new internal jugular line placement, to
assess for position.

Technique: Single AP radiograph of the chest.

Findings:

There is a left-sided internal jugular line seen in situ with the tip
approximately at the cavoatrial junction.  There is no pneumothorax.  The
cardiomediastinal silhouette is unremarkable.  The lungs are clear.

REASON FOR EXAMINATION:  Nausea and vomiting, suspected small-bowel
obstruction.

Three supine views of the abdomen were reviewed.  There is no evidence of
bowel obstruction.  There is no air-fluid level.  There is no free air below
the diaphragm.  Degenerative changes of the spine and the sacroiliac joints
are demonstrated.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of small-bowel obstruction.

HISTORY:  ___ female with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting.  Evaluate
for obstruction.

COMPARISON:  ___.

SUPINE ABDOMEN:  There is a relative paucity of bowel gas centrally, without
definite evidence of obstruction or ileus, as air and stool is seen throughout
the colon.  There is no supine evidence of free intraperitoneal air.  There is
no pneumatosis.  Linear foci of calcifications are seen along the soft tissues
of the lateral abdominal wall on the right, and may reflect either soft tissue
calcifications, or may be external to the patient.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been vomiting for six days now. I can’t keep anything down—not even water. I’ve barely eaten since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is the vomit bloody or does it look like food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. It looks like the soup I tried to eat or sometimes greenish. I also feel feverish—my brother had a sore throat, but no one else is sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any pain in your belly or when you pee?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I pee a lot and feel urgency, but no burning. My belly doesn’t hurt much, but I’ve had this constant body pain—worse than usual. It’s my fibromyalgia flaring up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You also mentioned headaches and weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, headache feels like my blood pressure is high. And I’ve lost about 25 pounds—mostly from not eating and my cellulitis episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your vitals and get some fluids into you. You look a bit dry. Since your IV access is tricky, we placed a line in your neck to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That neck line feels strange, but I’ll take it if it helps. I just want to stop throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Zofran for nausea and morphine for pain. You haven’t vomited since arriving, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a little better, but still nauseous. Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s wait a few hours. We want to make sure your stomach settles. We also ordered blood and urine tests to check for infection and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work shows you’re dehydrated but no signs of kidney issues. Your phenytoin level is very low—this could increase seizure risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. I haven’t taken my meds in three days because I vomited them. I haven’t had a seizure in years, but I’m scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving IV phenytoin to bring your levels up. We’ll recheck tomorrow. You’re also on Coumadin, and your INR is low—so we restarted that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about the nausea? Is it a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray—no blockage. Most likely viral gastroenteritis or gastroparesis. We’re giving IV fluids, Zofran, and Reglan to help your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Reglan? I’ve never taken that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps with stomach motility. You’ll take it by mouth once you can keep pills down. We also started Protonix to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I have new pain—left lower belly. Not sharp, but constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed. You’re not running a fever, and your vitals are stable. We’d like to do a CT scan to check, but we need IV contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can’t you use the neck line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unfortunately, it wasn’t placed for contrast. And we understand you don’t want to try drinking contrast—it might make you vomit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I can’t risk it. Could this be fibromyalgia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Fibromyalgia can cause widespread and abdominal discomfort. We’ll monitor. If pain worsens, we may reconsider imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine test came back with signs of infection—white blood cells and bacteria. We sent a culture to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That explains the frequent urination. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a urinary tract infection. Not severe, but we’ll treat it. Once we get the culture result, we’ll pick the right antibiotic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had UTIs before. Will I need IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. If you can keep pills down, we’ll switch to oral meds. Your nausea is improving, so that’s promising.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your phenytoin level is now in the normal range. We’ll switch you back to your regular oral dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Any update on the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The culture grew Proteus mirabilis, a common UTI bug. It’s sensitive to several antibiotics, including ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I take that when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for seven days. We’ll also keep you on Reglan for a while to help with stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your belly pain has improved, and you’ve had bowel movements. That’s a good sign—no obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is almost gone. I even sipped some broth yesterday without vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral—oxycodone and morphine as needed. Your fibromyalgia pain seems under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried about the IV morphine making me nauseous again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on a nicotine patch to help with smoking. You’ve been using the gum when cravings hit—good job staying on the floor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s hard, but I don’t want to risk falling or getting sick outside. I’m trying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow. You’re afebrile, drinking fluids, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I go home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same doses for blood pressure, thyroid, and seizure meds. You’ll take ciprofloxacin for the UTI and Reglan for nausea. Pain meds are reduced to lower doses as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Coumadin? Do I need a blood test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Get your INR and phenytoin level checked in one week. Call your PCP to send the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I start vomiting again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if you have fever over 101, severe pain, blood in stool, or can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You’ve improved significantly—eating, drinking, and stable vitals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep taking your meds, stay hydrated, and follow up on your labs. We’ll see you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Nurse will bring your discharge papers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we like to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old female was admitted for nausea and vomiting lasting six days, with inability to tolerate oral intake and associated dehydration. She also reported urinary frequency and urgency, left lower quadrant pain, and worsening fibromyalgia pain. Initial concerns included bowel obstruction and low phenytoin levels due to missed doses. Abdominal imaging showed no obstruction. She was treated with IV fluids, antiemetics, and IV phenytoin, which was later transitioned to oral therapy as levels normalized. A urine culture confirmed Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infection, treated with ciprofloxacin. Her nausea improved with Reglan and bowel rest, and she gradually resumed oral intake. Pain was managed with IV then oral opioids. She remained seizure-free and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to complete antibiotics, continue Reglan, and follow up on INR and phenytoin levels in one week.
